clinicalPearls: Cholesterol embolisation syndrome occurs when cholesterol crystals are showered from ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques into small distal arteries, most often after angiography, vascular surgery or anticoagulation in a patient with widespread atherosclerosis.
The classic triad is livedo reticularis, blue or discoloured toes with preserved peripheral pulses, and acute or subacute kidney injury developing days to weeks after an inciting vascular event.
Peripheral eosinophilia is a valuable, though transient, clue and helps distinguish atheroembolism from contrast-induced nephropathy, which typically follows a different time course.
Preserved distal pulses despite ischaemic digits are characteristic because the occlusion is at the microvascular level rather than in the large conduit arteries.
Hollenhorst plaques, bright refractile cholesterol crystals seen at retinal arteriolar bifurcations on fundoscopy, provide supportive evidence of systemic atheroembolism.
Renal impairment often progresses in a stepwise fashion over weeks reflecting recurrent showers, in contrast to the rapid rise and recovery of contrast nephropathy.
Definitive diagnosis requires demonstration of biconvex, needle-shaped cholesterol clefts within occluded small arteries on biopsy of skin, muscle or kidney, though the diagnosis is often clinical.

Management is largely supportive with aggressive control of atherosclerotic risk factors and statin therapy; anticoagulation may worsen the syndrome by destabilising plaques and is generally avoided if possible.
reference.pathophysiology: Cholesterol embolisation syndrome arises when the fibrous cap of an ulcerated atheromatous plaque, typically in the aorta or large arteries, is disrupted, releasing cholesterol crystals and atheromatous debris into the circulation. These crystals lodge in small arteries and arterioles of 100-200 micrometres, causing mechanical occlusion followed by a foreign-body inflammatory reaction with endothelial injury, giant-cell infiltration and intimal proliferation that further narrows the lumen. The resulting distal ischaemia produces the cutaneous, renal, gastrointestinal, muscular and neurological manifestations. Because the process is showered and inflammatory rather than a single large occlusion, organ dysfunction typically evolves subacutely and in a stepwise manner. Plaque disruption is frequently precipitated by intravascular instrumentation, vascular surgery, thrombolysis or anticoagulation, the last of which is thought to prevent protective thrombus formation over ulcerated plaque and allow continued embolisation.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and other thrombotic microangiopathies
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count looking for peripheral eosinophilia
Renal function, urinalysis and inflammatory markers (often raised ESR/CRP, hypocomplementaemia)
Skin, muscle or renal biopsy demonstrating cholesterol clefts in occluded vessels
Vascular imaging of the aorta and large arteries to identify the embolic source
Autoimmune and vasculitis serology to exclude mimics
Blood cultures and echocardiography where endocarditis is a consideration
redFlags: Progressive acute kidney injury following angiography or vascular surgery
Digital ischaemia or necrosis with intact peripheral pulses
Mesenteric ischaemia presenting with abdominal pain or gastrointestinal bleeding
Neurological deficits suggesting cerebral or spinal atheroembolism
Rapid multi-organ deterioration after an intravascular procedure
reference.prognosis: Cholesterol embolisation syndrome carries significant morbidity and mortality, particularly when renal and mesenteric involvement occur; renal recovery is often incomplete and many patients progress to chronic kidney disease, with outcome reflecting the extent of atherosclerotic burden and organ ischaemia.
pitfalls: Mistaking the renal injury for contrast-induced nephropathy and missing the atheroembolic time course
Attributing blue toes to large-vessel occlusion despite the preserved pulses
Continuing or starting anticoagulation, which may perpetuate embolisation
Overlooking eosinophilia and Hollenhorst plaques as diagnostic clues
Misdiagnosing the multisystem picture as a primary systemic vasculitis
